transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-03-17
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jenna Ortiz (Aurelia CTO), Marcus Lee (Aurelia Lead Eng), Priya Nair (Aurelia Sec), Tom Becker (PM), Alex Ruiz (Redwood CSM briefly)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
 - Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/textgen basics, streaming behavior, parameter impacts, and retry/backoff patterns.
 - Customer questions on latency targets, data residency/SOC2, and integration timelines.
 - Redwood to send code snippet, pricing examples, and schedule deeper technical session.

Topics covered: hosted chat API, streaming, param tuning, idempotency/retries, console cost controls, security/compliance notes.

Action items (captured during call): see metadata field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, AE on the account. We have Samir the SE with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Jenna Ortiz: Good, thanks. We wanted to see a short walkthrough — mainly hosted chat, streaming behavior, and how to tune responses. We're evaluating for a clinical triage assistant prototype.
[00:16] Marcus Lee: Also curious about latency tradeoffs given we're targeting sub-300ms for short prompts.
[00:22] Samir Patel: Great. I'll demo live and show console bits. Quick qual — what's your expected qps and typical prompt lengths?
[00:28] Tom Becker: For POC maybe 10–20 rps, but eventual product could be 200–500. Prompt lengths vary, usually 30–120 tokens user + system instructions.
[00:35] Priya Nair: And security — we need SOC2, KMS, and no cross-customer data leakage. We'll ask more later.
[00:42] Maya Chen: Totally. High level: hosted API gives you fast onboarding, streaming for low latency perception, plus console for per-route cost/latency. We'll show safe defaults for retries and backoff too.
[00:52] Samir Patel: Alright I'm sharing my screen — starting with a simple chat request. I'm using the Redwood hosted chat endpoint, streaming enabled. Code snippet first — Node example.
[01:05] Samir Patel: (reads) const response = await redwood.chat.create({ model: 'rwd-chat-1-large', streaming: true, messages: [...], temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 200 });
[01:14] Marcus Lee: Quick Q: rwd-chat-1-large — is that pinned to a particular backend or does Redwood route?
[01:19] Samir Patel: Good question. Hosted model names are logical and we route to best-fit variants. You can pin a specific variant if needed for latency determinism. There's also a latency profile in the console.
[01:29] Jenna Ortiz: When you say streaming, is that chunked tokens or server-sent events?
[01:32] Samir Patel: It streams chunks over SSE or websockets depending on SDK; basically partial token frames so front-ends can render progressively.
[01:40] [00:40] (note: small timestamp jump/mislabel)
[01:45] Samir Patel: For short prompts streaming gets you perceived latency improvement because you start seeing tokens immediately rather than waiting for model decode to finish. But there are tradeoffs around connection management and downsteam buffering.
[01:55] Tom Becker: How do we handle retries if a stream disconnects mid-response? We can't double-post the same message to user.
[02:01] Samir Patel: Great — two patterns. 1) Idempotency keys for request-level retries; if you retry, Redwood can resume or deduplicate based on idempotency metadata. 2) Short-lived prefix caching: if the prefix is identical we can use KV cache to resume from last known token offset — more advanced and typically used on Dedicated/private deployments but we have hosted options too.
[02:20] Priya Nair: That prefix cache part — is that considered PII exposure? Concern about cached data location.
[02:25] Maya Chen: Good flag. For hosted we default to ephemeral caches with customer isolation; for strict compliance customers we recommend Dedicated or Private where you can control KMS and cache residency. We'll include specifics in the security pack.
[02:36] Jenna Ortiz: Can you show how temperature and top_k/top_p impact output?
[02:40] Samir Patel: Sure — demo time. I'll run the same prompt with temp 0.0, 0.6, 1.0.
[02:46] [03:00] Samir (demo): Temp 0.0 gives deterministic short reply — useful for instruction following. Temp 0.6 introduces variety, better for natural language suggestions. Temp 1.0 is more diverse but sometimes hallucinated.
[03:10] Marcus Lee: Do you have recommended defaults for triage assistant? We want accurate short responses.
[03:14] Maya Chen: For triage I'd start 0.0–0.3, and set max_tokens to 80 to encourage brevity. Also consider n-best or beam alternatives if you need structured suggestions.
[03:25] Tom Becker: What's the per-token cost delta with higher temps? I thought cost is per token regardless of temp?
[03:29] Samir Patel: Cost is per token generated/consumed; temperature doesn't change compute linearly but it can change length of outputs and tendency to sample longer continuations. So indirectly affects cost. Console Optimize has per-route token insights so you can correlate param choices with spend.
[03:44] Jenna Ortiz: Show the console please.
[03:46] Samir Patel: Switching to Console — here's model catalog with performance profiles, per-route latency percentile graphs, and token cost breakdown. You can set per-route limits (max tokens, concurrency) and configure suggested batching if you want to economize.
[03:58] [04:10] Samir: (pointing) This route shows 95th p latency at 220ms for the model variant we've selected — matches your sub-300ms target for small prompts. But note, under load percentiles widen.
[04:21] Marcus Lee: How do we simulate 200–500 rps? Can we run a burst test?
[04:25] Samir Patel: Yes we offer sandbox load tests; for Dedicated we'd recommend a reservation. For hosted we can advise on throttles, autoscaling suggestions, and graceful fallback policies to cheaper variants in the routing layer.
[04:36] Priya Nair: Regarding data retention — does Redwood keep transcripts? We need logs for evaluation but also need a retention window and deletion policy.
[04:44] Maya Chen: Hosted keeps request/response logs for X days by default (we'll confirm exact retention in the docs) but you can request shorter retention, and enterprise customers have options for disabled logging. We'll send SOC2 and retention doc.
[04:55] Tom Becker: On retries/backoff — do you have recommended backoff timings? Exponential plus jitter?
[05:00] Samir Patel: Yes exponential backoff with full jitter typically. For interactive flows we recommend quick initial retry (200–500ms) with a small cap to avoid long waits. For idempotent ops you can be more aggressive.
[05:12] Marcus Lee: If a retry results in a ghost duplicate message because user already saw partial tokens, any suggestions?
[05:17] Samir Patel: Client-side can track message hashes and server idempotency to dedupe. Another pattern: server returns final token index so you know where to resume — but that is advanced and we've seen teams prefer deterministic end-to-end idempotency keys.
[05:30] [05:35] (brief crosstalk)
[05:38] Jenna Ortiz: Can you speak to model rollouts — if you push a model update does latency change? We want stable behavior.
[05:44] Maya Chen: We support pinned model versions and controlled rollouts (canary/A-B). Console shows performance deltas and automatic fallback to previous variants if regressions detected. You can set quality gates tied to eval prompts so a bad rollout is auto-rolled back.
[05:58] Tom Becker: Nice. Can we do evals via the console?
[06:00] Samir Patel: Yes there's an Optimize dashboard for prompt sets and quality regression alerts. You upload reference prompts and expected outputs; the platform runs continuous checks.
[06:09] Marcus Lee: For the triage domain, we will need medically-sensitive text in prompts. What about redaction or PII scrubbing?
[06:16] Priya Nair: (adds) Also encryption at rest in hosted? Key separation?
[06:20] Maya Chen: Hosted uses provider-managed encryption by default; for key separation and bring-your-own-key you can opt for Dedicated or Private. We do offer limited PII scrubbing helpers and we can integrate with customer-side preprocessors. We'll include specifics in the security packet.
[06:31] [06:40] Samir: Back to practical SDK examples — here's a retry wrapper pattern. Pseudocode: try request with idempotency header; on stream disconnect, attempt resume if server signals resume token else re-run with same idempotency key and dedupe on client.
[06:55] Marcus Lee: Could you paste that snippet after the call?
[06:58] Samir Patel: Absolutely, will include in the follow-up.
[07:02] Jenna Ortiz: A question about multi-turn — do you recommend sending full history each time or using server-side conversation state?
[07:08] Samir Patel: Two options: 1) send condensed history client-side, which gives you full control but more tokens; 2) server conversation state where we keep a short KV reference and you fetch/resume — hosted supports lightweight conversation ids but for strict data residency prefer Dedicated/Private. There's a trade-off in token cost vs DB plumbing complexity.
[07:25] Tom Becker: If the conversation state is stored, who can access it? Role-based access?
[07:29] Maya Chen: Yes RBAC in Console for routes and tokens; for hosted we isolate customer namespaces. For enterprise customers, there's finer control and audit logs.
[07:39] [08:00] (small pause while Samir switches to a small live demo of degraded stream)
[08:05] Samir Patel: I'm going to simulate a dropped connection. Watch the stream — it cuts at char 142. Client retries with same idempotency, server returns 'duplicate detected' header and we receive final completed payload.
[08:22] Marcus Lee: Nice, so user won't get doubled content.
[08:25] Samir Patel: Right; but note that resume behaviors vary by model and config — we'll document recommended headers and error codes.
[08:33] Priya Nair: Where can we find the SLA for hosted?
[08:36] Maya Chen: Hosted SLA is available for enterprise tiers; we'll send the SLA doc. The hosted free tier has no SLA.
[08:44] Jenna Ortiz: Do you have guidance for batching user messages? For our use case we need per-message low-latency but also want to batch low-priority requests.
[08:52] Samir Patel: You can configure adaptive batching at the routing layer — group low-priority calls into batches when latency SLO allows. Console Optimize will suggest batching thresholds by analyzing historical arrival patterns.
[09:05] Tom Becker: Anything in the console about cost projections?
[09:08] Samir Patel: Yes per-route projected spend with sliders for param changes (lower max_tokens, change temperature) — useful for cost experiments.
[09:18] [09:30] (brief mention of integration with SSO)
[09:33] Priya Nair: We need SAML SSO for team access. Support that?
[09:36] Maya Chen: Yes, SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning available for enterprise accounts. We'll add our SSO setup guide to the follow-up.
[09:45] Marcus Lee: If we start POC, what's the fastest path: hosted sandbox or Dedicated trial?
[09:50] Maya Chen: Hosted sandbox is fastest — you get tokens, quickstart repo, and can run smoke tests. If you need stricter controls (BYOK, network restrictions) we can discuss a Dedicated pilot.
[10:00] Jenna Ortiz: Let's talk timeline — we want to surface a POC in 6 weeks.
[10:04] Maya Chen: That sounds doable. Next step: we'll send a POC plan and pricing ranges for hosted; Samir will prep a deeper technical session focusing on your scale and latency targets.
[10:13] Samir Patel: Also we'll include a short benchmark script and sample load generator config so you can simulate 200–500 rps in a sandbox.
[10:22] [10:30] (client side question on rate limits)
[10:32] Samir Patel: For rate limits we support per-account and per-token quotas; you can request soft increases during POC.
[10:39] Tom Becker: Any tricky gotchas we should watch for?
[10:42] Samir Patel: Watch prompt length and repeated system prompts — they increase token usage. Also be mindful of streaming reconnection logic; naive retries can double-cost if dedupe isn't implemented.
[10:55] Jenna Ortiz: Priya will compile security checklist items and send to Maya; Priya?
[10:59] Priya Nair: Yes, I'll send our SOC2, PII handling, and KMS questions.
[11:04] Maya Chen: Great. To wrap up I'll summarize and list the follow-ups.
[11:09] (Recap)
[11:12] Maya Chen: Recap: 1) We showed hosted chat streaming, param impacts (temp, max_tokens), and retry patterns. 2) Console has per-route latency and cost, Optimize suggests batching and token controls. 3) Security/compliance options include different retention and Dedicated/Private for BYOK. 4) Next steps: send code snippets, security pack, pricing examples, and schedule deep dive.
[11:34] Jenna Ortiz: Thanks all — that helps. We'll review and get the security questions over.
[11:38] Marcus Lee: Thanks — looking forward to the deep dive.
[11:41] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items in the next 48 hours.
[11:45] (Meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quirks: speaker labels were auto-assigned, timestamps approximate and occasionally misaligned; some product names transcribed roughly (rwd-chat-1-large might appear different in raw audio).
